Apple officially launched the Apple Upgrade leasing programme today, and it operates exactly as we had anticipated earlier. Although the programme makes products more affordable through monthly instalments, it may trap users in an endless cycle of leasing.

The reason is that, compared to the iPhone Upgrade Program it partially replaces, users do not actually own the device after the lease term ends……

At a time when Apple product prices keep hitting new highs, the appeal of making products more accessible is undeniable. Looking purely at the monthly payments, the Apple Upgrade programme does achieve this.

For example, you can lease a MacBook Pro with 16GB of memory and 1TB of storage for as little as US$38.99 per month. This approach enables more consumers to get their hands on more Apple products, which is absolutely a good thing.

Hidden concerns of the Apple Upgrade programme

However, the worry is precisely what I foresaw last week: users will use this programme just like leasing a car. Although you can choose to pay a lump sum at the end of the lease to fully own the car, almost no one does that. The vast majority of people who lease cars return the car and lease a new one, starting a fresh cycle.

The same situation could arise with the Apple Upgrade programme. To fully own the product, you must pay a residual amount equal to the difference between the product's original price and the total lease payments you have already made.

Let's use the MacBook Pro mentioned above as an example to see how it works in practice (amounts rounded to the nearest dollar):

36-month plan

  • Monthly payment: US$38.99
  • Total payment over the entire lease term: US$1,403
  • Residual amount required to buy out the device: US$585

24-month plan

  • Monthly payment: US$53.99
  • Total payment over the entire lease term: US$1,295
  • Residual amount required to buy out the device: US$703

For someone who originally cannot afford to buy the device outright, coming up with that sum of money on the spot is no easy feat. Unless they have been saving up that difference throughout the lease term, they will most likely be unable to cope when the time comes. In that case, the most probable outcome is that they will start a new leasing cycle all over again.

The smart approach (if you can afford it)

If you can afford a higher monthly outlay, the smart move is to restructure the programme yourself into something equivalent to the IUP.

While paying Apple's monthly lease instalments, you also put money into a savings account each month to cover the residual amount due at the end. Taking the 36-month MBP lease as an example, the numbers would work out as follows:

  • Monthly lease payment: US$38.99
  • Monthly savings contribution: US$16.26
  • Total monthly outlay: US$55.25
  • Total amount paid to Apple: US$1,403
  • Total amount saved for the residual: US$585.36 (plus any interest earned)

Ryan Lounsbury's top-rated comment

I might use this leasing programme to buy an iPhone. I upgrade my phone every 12 to 24 months. Assuming there's zero interest, I could return the device when the term is up and switch to the latest model without having to fork out the full cost of the device in one go. Given my upgrade habits, this approach makes a lot of sense for me.

However, Apple has built a catch into the Upgrade/leasing programme—it requires you to select and activate the device through a designated carrier. I've been using Mint Mobile for years, but if I have to do that just to use the leasing programme, I can't take advantage of it, and I'd also be hit with a small fee for not activating it through a 'blessed' carrier, which is really off-putting.

Then you can use the money you've saved to pay that US$585 residual, and the device is entirely yours.

Of course, if you really want to upgrade to a new device, you can absolutely sell the one you now own and apply for a new lease. The amount you get from a private sale will very likely be enough to cover the new residual, so you just put that money straight into your savings account, and your actual monthly outlay is reduced to just the lease instalment.

How do you plan to fund your future Apple purchases? Feel free to share your thoughts in the comments.
